And according to what he's writing -- in the English version you can't see this on the screen. Maybe in your version you can't see it either. You have to look at the last page. That's it. It's not the last page yet.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have the document now. You see that it's a handwritten document which states that General Praljak sent a message himself that he would annihilate if they didn't accept the decisions of the HZ HB. It's a bit woolly, but one could draw the conclusion that you made them understand -- the other part was made to understand that if they did not accept the decisions, they would be in a certain way destroyed. Now, maybe it's Colonel Siljeg who harped on it, who -- what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained to Their Honours that I was sent down there by Mr. Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman to calm the already -- the conflict that had already broken out in Gornji Vakuf. And on behalf of the HVO there, you had the Deputy Chief of the Main Staff Milivoj Petkovic, Mr. Andric, and the commander of the operative zone, Mr. Siljeg. They were the commanders. I don't want to say that my influence on them was small, no. However, since the Muslims had been entrenching themselves for months and had brought the HVO into a situation they couldn't get out of in Gornji Vakuf, I accepted the explanation given by the two commanders to the effect that the military situation there was untenable as far as the HVO was concerned. In another document and in the document of Hadzihasanovic about what they had asked for, the two commanders had asked for at a joint meeting, it conveyed what I told them to ask for in great measure, and that was a truce, that the trenches be filled in, that there be joint patrols set up by both military police forces, that a curfew be introduced, and so on and so forth. And let me just say -- let me just finish here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the second document is going to exemplify what you just said. Look at the P01350. This is a document which we've already seen. This is a report from Mr. Lukic, dated 29 January 1993, and there was a meeting which was held on the 27th of January where you were attending with Mr. Coric. And you answered questions which were asked of you, and one sees that after that that just as you've said, there were some check-points with the HVO and the ABiH. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But allow me to finish what I was saying. To go back to the previous document, certainly the word "pregazen," "overrun", doesn't come from me. It is a word used by Mr. Siljeg, and that's quite certain, the word "pregazen." And I certainly have no [realtime transcript read in error "to"] right to ask about any decisions of the HZ HB. I had nothing to do with that. I succeeded in what I was there to do, and it is A --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise but there's a mistake in the transcript which is important. On page 51, line 17 and 18, General Praljak said: "I certainly did not have the right to ask for any decisions of the HZ HB," and in the transcript the not -- the negative has been left out and therefore reads differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and speak not so fast and be a bit more brief.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't use the word "pregaziti," overrun, or run over. Second, I made no suggestions with respect to decisions being made by the HZ HB government. Third, it wasn't an ultimatum. It was a pure military request which I supported. If the soldiers of the BH Army failed to leave their positions up on the hills which they had taken control of in Vakuf -- by which they have taken control of the HVO in Vakuf, that, yes, was my position. The other proposals were as I made them. And the most important thing is that when this limited military goal was achieved, which is termed "active defence," by the firm position that I had taken, the attack on Vakuf was stopped. So the defeat of the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf could have been realised in the space of a single day. Since that was not the HVO's objective despite heavy HVO losses and the great desire on the part of the soldiers to finish up their military victory, I used my authority to stop this on the 23rd of January, 1991, and once again called for the establishment of a -- joint check-points, to deal with the conflict and to see what could be done next. And here in this document P01350, it says that a check-point was indeed established and so on and so forth. So at this meeting I explained to the military policemen, and a lot of them were killed up there, what the position was that I brought from Zagreb and how it was to be implemented. And then further on in the text we can see the sensitivity of conflicts of this kind and that it was the Muslims in the military police of the Croatian Defence Council were not being sent into the field to prevent them from shooting at their own people. So this is highly sensitive ethnically speaking. In human terms as well, but also in military terms. You can't do what the BH Army did in Gornji Vakuf with Hanefija and all the rest of them without the -- given the opportunity to respond. That was my position and I've described all the rest of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution say that you took part in the joint criminal enterprise and perpetrating the crimes, that you facilitated them, that you supported them by planifying -- planning, approving, preparing, supporting, ordering and/or directing operations and military actions during and in the framework which these crimes were perpetrated. In a word, the Prosecution says that you directed military operations which led to crimes. And he alleges in the pre-trial brief, in a document we will see now, P03026 ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, this is a document of the 30th of June, 1993. The author of the document is Mr. Siljeg, and this is being sent -- this document is being sent to the authorities, in particular Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and this document seems to mention you, because there is Brada, which is mentioned. So it says that you have taken recognisance of the report on the situation in Mostar and of the order which comes from the defence department, chief of defence, and the president of the HVO, of the HV, Mr. Prlic. So Stojic and Prlic -- it is I who has say so. So therefore the following measures are requested: First, order to take Blagaj to Obradovic; two, at all costs prevent their linking between Mostar and Jablanica; and, three, start working as at Breznica. According to you, what does exactly -- what does this report say exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me answer that point. You were able to see from the dozens of orders what -- what they were, what my conduct was both with the prisoners in Capljina, the helicopters and the wounded and the road of salvation, and the forcible disbanding of the camp in Dretelj with the Serbs in 1992 and so on and so forth, and I reject all possibility put forward by the Prosecutor in this section. And here on the 30th of June I was on Boksevica hill, and you know where Boksevica is to be found. It is above -- or, rather, between Konjic and Jablanica. And on Boksevica hill we had our defence lines there which were being held only because -- only so that from the region of Slatina -- is it Slatina? Yes, Slatina. That the population -- that the Croatian population could be pulled out of that area and the remaining soldiers after the BH Army in Konjic had done what it had done. Has that all been interpreted? I'm a soldier up there, an ordinary soldier, on guard, at my position just like any other rank and file soldier. That's the authority -- I had authority but no other competencies. The guys just listened to me. And Siljeg came to visit us, and he says that the BH Army had attacked all the HVO lines on the 30th of June, when they attacked north camp and killed the people there, when they attacked Stolac and so on and so forth. And I say to him in an ordinary conversation as a responses to what was going to happen next, in my opinion Obradovic should take control of Blagaj, and that's what I think today as well, and he should have deployed the tanks that were used against the Chetniks because now we were facing a BH Army aggression, a crystal clear BH Army aggression. No doubt about that. And we should attack the army from the south of Mostar. And secondly, which was logical in military terms, to try and cut off all communication between Mostar and Jablanica. And similarly, that Dreznica, in military terms, because you could move towards Mostar from Dreznica, from the right bank of the Neretva River to prevent that. That was my military advice, the military advice I gave to Siljeg, and he conveyed that correctly to Bruno Stojic and Milivoj Petkovic. And I was up on that hill, and I stayed there until the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be as synthetic as possible, as concise as possible. You take a lot of time while there are other elements, items on which I need to know your position, and they are just as important, perhaps even more important. There is a witness, but I won't give his name because he's a protected witness and part of what he said was in a closed session and he might be identified, so this witness said this, on pages 12266. He heard you say something. This is what you've said: "We agreed with the Serbs. We made an agreement which is to say that we were going to provoke them by artillery shelling at Agido [phoen]," excuse my pronunciation, "on their part through artillery shelling they will destroy Stolac, all the balijas, and raze Stolac to the ground." This is what he said. Where you're sitting now, this is what he said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was nothing but a criminal and a liar, the most terrible sort of that. And you don't remember all the documents that have been presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... said, he's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after that, from the office of President Mesic, not of President Tudjman, you heard that on that day and a day later I was in Zagreb, at a meeting there, and the documents exist and have been admitted. He was a liar and you received that. Why you keep on asking me about that. Second of all, how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, General Praljak. I have to ask you such questions, because when the Judges will meet together at the end of the trial and they will have to apprise on that, they will have also judge what the witnesses said, what you said, what the Prosecution has said, what other people has said, and all this will have to be weighed. So if I don't ask you this question today, now that you are facing me, I wouldn't be doing my job. Therefore, this is the reason why I am obliged to tell you this, because this is part of the indictment charge, and you have to say so on that particular day or the next day you were this or that meeting. All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, please. Your Honours, I remember things very well. My brain is still working, only not as good as it used to. That witness said as follows: The HVO launched an action in the direction of Stolac. Two hours into that operation a group of the HVO troops returned. They could not proceed because it was pounded from all sides, and they had sent him. Mind you him, let's not mention his name. And that group told him this: "Go to Capljina, to the Main Staff, and request assistance." And then he actually enters the staff, the operations staff. There he is standing behind a wall. You can't see him. There are no guards, nothing of the sort. It's as simple as that. It's as if he was in a bistro in France, entering a bistro to have a cup of coffee. And there's Praljak there saying what he's saying. Praljak can't see him, but he can see Praljak. He can hear Praljak. Listen here. This is an ultimate nonsense. That person should be arrested and convicted to two years of prison. And if this had been done to every false witness, these trials would look entirely different than they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a Prosecution witness, and therefore I had to tell you, I had to remind you. On this particular theme of military operations I have one last document which is also important, P04265. 4265.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Judge Antonetti to allow me to say something else. After the event related by that person, the HVO armed a brigade of the BH Army in the territory, the Bregava Brigade. Please, really. I'm familiar with this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is a document that comes from the HVO, 17th of August, 1993, at the time you were exercising the command. This is addressed to the Main Staff, and it is addressed to you since you're in charge, and the chief. And Napalm bombs are mentioned. The bomb was dropped at a height of 600 metres. According to what we understand, one bomb was dropped and the others went. It's quite possible. We don't know whether the bomb that was dropped fell in a river and what happened to the others. We don't quite know what happened to the others. This is a bit of a mystery. As far as you know, if you need to drop a Napalm bomb, you need a fairly large sized aeroplane or helicopter. I don't know. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sent to the Main Staff of the HVO, to the chief. I was the commander thereof. So this detail is wrong, but never mind that. A month elapsed for this when I learned -- learned that they used some sort of an aircraft, farming aircraft, and launched a bomb. First of all, it has nothing whatsoever to do with Napalm. Napalm bombs can be manufactured by only very technically developed states. And when I inquired about what sort of Napalm they were mentioning, they had actually mixed something that looked like a Molotov cocktail. It is not known whether the first one fell into the Neretva, and nothing is known about the second one, whether it was activated at all. In any case, you've seen a document by which I had forbidden any sorties or flights after I'd seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to the witness's blatant mischaracterization of what the document that's in front of him says. Now, he's just claimed that neither of the bombs deployed properly. The fact is the document on its face says that one of them did work properly and was deployed in the area of Mahala in Mostar and that it affected an area of about 500, 600 metres. So if he's claiming that neither of these worked, it's false because the document says otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that this is the argument. Everyone has a right to understand the document as it is. Mr. Praljak, on one way, I on the other, Mr. Stringer on his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, this is exactly one of the questions you could have put during your cross-examination. You may not agree with him, and you can turn to Mr. Praljak during your cross-examination and say, "This is not right for such and such a reason." Mr. Praljak, a witness came to testify here who mentioned this bomb. The witness said that there had been a bomb, and he fired 15 shots against the plane with his rifle, and Samir died after the bomb was dropped. You're telling us today that you discovered this question of the Napalm bomb one month later. This is precisely what you're telling us, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the first truth. Second of all, I did not really investigate it into its coverage. The second thing that I'm refuting, and I know this with a hundred percent accuracy, it was not a Napalm. That Lovric, he didn't know how to draft a document let alone to be able to tell what Napalm was. Please, Your Honours, if Napalm was to be deployed across 500 or 600 metres of space, then 300 people would have burnt down not just one man -- one person. I could have dropped a normal bomb from my Air Force on the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the laws of war, but I didn't do that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's assume that this is not Napalm but a shell. So you are telling us, since you were the commander you were not aware of this, you may be right, or you were not well informed, but in Mostar at the time the international community observers were there with their binoculars. There were spies. Everybody was there and everybody was observing what was happening, and a small private aeroplane dropped something without the person in charge of the HVO being made aware of this. This is possible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't understand your understanding of the army. There is an aircraft or air force commander. Do you think that the commander of the French air force knows what every single person in every battalion does? Every commander is responsible, every soldier is responsible, every soldier is aware of the rules of war because they have been issued with booklets. Please. And second of all -- please allow me, Judge Trechsel. Are you saying, are you claiming that a bomb should not be thrown on the positions of the BiH army at the moment when that army is attacking us? Could you please put that in the decision, in the judgement? We were allowed to throw bombs. We were not allowed to throw Napalm, but we did not have a Napalm in any case and this is a responsibility I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you are quite right. According to the laws of war, you are entitled to drop bombs on the enemy. Nobody is challenging this. But in this document, the place where the bomb was dropped is mentioned, and this is Mahala. You know that there were civilians in this area. This is what the question is about. Seemingly, if you join this up or relate this to the witness said, that Samir died as a result, maybe Samir was a soldier of the ABiH, but maybe Samir was a civilian. Do you understand? So you're right when you say that one is entitled to drop bombs when there is fighting, but the problem is that some people are protected, and in Mahala, as far as I know, there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH army was also there in Mahala. In Mahala there were combat positions of the BH Army from which every offensive was launched in the direction of Hum and elsewhere. And this is a fact. The army that holds civilians in their -- in the area where they were -- their combat position, is that war crimes. Muslims did that in Mostar, in Sarajevo. That was their tactic, that's how they waged the war, civilians and troops being mixed in order to achieve a higher number of wounded civilians, and then the other side would be accused of committing immoral acts. Despite that, there were no more sorties after that, and you saw a document in which I said, No, only upon my approval or for the wounded, because even the rights that stemmed from the rules of war I did not use in order to avoid any civilian victims, and there were very few civilian casualties in Mostar as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the next topic. We have a request from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you remind me of the position and rank of Mr. Miroslav Lovric?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the air defence. I'm talking about the overall strength of the air defence, and I don't know what his rank was, to be honest. He was the commander of air defence. In other words, he had the right to issue decision either in agreement with the commander of the operative zone or the commander of a brigade. At that particular moment, the commander of the Main Staff did not have to know anything about that, because at that moment given the communications as they were, the commander of the Main Staff was in Vakuf fighting every day for 20 hours, and in the south of Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. I put the question to you, because if I have understood correctly, you said that this was not a Napalm bomb but some other product. Have I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that. Those people did not have a clue about what Napalm was. Napalm could be produced by maybe 10 or 12 states that had high-technology. And if Napalm indeed had been thrown, everything within the radius of 500 or 600 metres would be ablaze, not just one man. And we don't even know whether he was a member of the BH Army or whether he was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm now coming to my last question. This commander who prepares a report for the commander or the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, he talks about weapons that don't exist. Is it customary when such reports are sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Mindua, the great Churchill said there are three situations in which everybody lies. First, after a hunt. Second, on the eve of the elections, and thirdly, in war. In war, everybody lies. Reports are being blown up out of proportions. The positions are mistakenly represented. By the nature of the beast, war is represented in all sorts of way. They want to portray their strength as being bigger than it is. They blow up the number of enemies killed out proportion. War is a situation in which everybody lies. In every war, in every army. Churchill was lied to. DeGaulle was lied to. You saw reports from the Second World War here near the Arden range. War is nothing but a pack of lies in reports and on papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going [previous translation continues]... not responsive to Judge Mindua's question. I think that answer is not responsive in the least to the question about reporting to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Mindua, this is what I'm saying. This was not Napalm. I checked that. And this person suggests that Napalm should be produced and enhanced. So if he had thrown it, he must have of had it. Why is he suggesting that it should be produced and enhanced? You either have it or not. You can't enhance it. This is a nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, according to the Prosecution, you commanded, facilitated, and supported the operations and activities of the military police of the HVO with which you pursued the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise. So you controlled -- you commanded and supported the operations of the military police, and in support of this we shall look at look at document P4125.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I shall first put my question. This document is dated the 12th of August, 1993. It stems from you, seemingly, because I think I recognise your signature. And it's a request for resources and equipment. All the forces should be gathered quickly and placed under the command of Colonel Obradovic, and you specify that the chiefs of the military police and the commanders of the police stations of Capljina, Citluk are in charge of executing the order, and you ask Colonel Obradovic to keep you informed on a regular basis. If we look at numeral 4, this seems to be stating that there is a link between you and the military police. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this order was drafted in connection with the order by the head of the defence department who had his own rights. This order was the product of an agreement between Mr. Stojic and myself, and it talks about a terrorist attack by a group of Muslim armed forces, Mostar Buna, Zitomislici, Capljina. Your Honours, you will remember the massacred bodies in the bodies in the barracks in Capljina. We had shown them here, and those were not soldiers. They were members of the HV [as interpreted], but they were carrying food. They were not armed. They were people who were in charge of the distribution of food. They were killed in the most beastly way. You had an opportunity to see the photos in this courtroom. In a situation when somebody gets behind your lines and infiltrates their terrorist group, interim orders are issued and you involve hunters, military police, you mobilise people, because after what you have seen the massacred bodies of the people who had been bringing food, I still adhere by this document. I stand by it. This document was sent to the military police based on the agreement between Mr. Stojic and myself, and you can see it in the preamble. This was our right, and this was also our duty. I was not in command over the military police save for the instances when it was resubordinated to me under lines. It was an institution parallel to the HVO and it was also connected with the defence department and this is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the record, page 65, line 1, the general said HVO, not the HV. He said that they were members of the HVO and not of the HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecution states as follows: You contributed to a system of mistreatment by controlling it, conducting it, assisting it and/or taking part in this. This system included a network of prisons, of concentration camps, and other detention centres used for the purpose of arresting, detaining, and incarcerating thousands of Muslims from Bosnia in -- in illegal and harsh conditions. There they were killed, mistreated, beaten, and brutalised. The Muslim detainees were automatically taken away from these detention centres by the forces of the HVO and forced to perform forced labour during which a great number of them were injured or killed. There is what -- this is how the Prosecution describes your participation in the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution quotes a document which we will see right away P04260. Mrs. Pinter is giving you the document. I thank her for facilitating everyone's work. You have the document on your screen very soon. This is a document which stems from you. We have it in the English version. It is addressed to the Rama Brigade, to the Uskoplje Brigade, and to the military police of Rama, and you say in this document that from the 17th of August, 1993, onwards, all prisoners are to be withdrawn from the tasks they have been given in your prospective zones of responsibility. So this document states that you put an end to a situation on the face of it. So what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep on repeating that you have to bear in mind the military situation at that moment or throughout that time. As you could see in the previous document, on the 17th of August, after I had been in the south of Mostar, I was in Rama. On the 16th of August I learned from Mr. Tole that some units had been taking prisoners. It was a brief piece of information that he had received from a prisoner. As soon as I received that order -- and until that moment I had never learned about that, or I had never seen anybody digging anything either in -- on the lines or around the lines. I immediately issued an order to the effect that the prisoners should not be used to work at all. No work at all. And immediately after that when I arrive in Grude, I issued an order that I don't have which applied to all operation zones, and by that order I banned any work in military units, and later on I saw some statements showing that some prisoners were actually not very happy with the news, because some used the opportunity to work privately. I didn't know anything about this. I issued two orders. The second is much longer, more extensive, and by these two orders I put a strict ban on any such practices. And as far as the detention centres are concerned, besides Heliodrom I was fully convinced that those were prisons. I did not have any control over the prisons. The prisons did not have anything to do with the Main Staff or the HVO army, when it came to their setting up control, investigations. And this is clear from the fact that we issued passes to the journalists. How -- somebody would have to be mad to do what is implied and then provide the journalists with passes to see what kind of a criminal he was. On the 20th of September, I sent my own soldiers to Dretelj, to the prison, because I was absolutely convinced that it was nothing else by -- but a prison, a regular prison. This is the information that I was privy to at the time. Everything else was subsequent information to the facts, and what I'm saying is the truth and can be proved by documents. I would not have allowed a TV crew, if a crime had been committed and if I'd known about that. I would not have been so crazy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned the Heliodrom. I would like to remind you but I'm sure you remember, there's a witness who came here, I'm not going to quote his name. I don't wish to jeopardise the protective measures he may have had. On page 14584 and following pages, this witness was unable to give us the exact date, but it was between the 17th and the 18th of August, 1993. Between the 16th and the 18th he was in the cinema of the Heliodrom, and you were in the refectory. He said he knew you because he'd seen you on photographs. He'd admired you during the fighting against the common enemy during the war, and he says that it was you. If you were at the Heliodrom in August of 1993, any reasonable trier of fact could infer thereof that since you were at the Heliodrom, you may have seen that there were people detained there. So my question is very simple. Were you there or weren't you there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. From the 17th I was in Rama. On the 16th I was in Rama. On the 18th I was in Rama-Prozor. I was never at Heliodrom. Or maybe in 2000 or 1998 I attended some celebration for the first time over there and Josip Praljak was there who was a relative of mine who I assume would have seen me. It would have been in some report. It would have said General Praljak was there. So regardless of our kinship relations, we met only after the war, because I didn't function in that way. I didn't function on -- based on family relations. I was never at Heliodrom during the war. When he says the 16th and 17th and 18th, where I was was that -- on the 15th I was in Grude with Bruno Stojic when he fainted because there was -- the BH Army offensive was routed in the south and I returned to Rama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Five minutes before we finish this session we will have a close session for the Defence of Mr. Stojic [as interpreted]. I think Mr. Stringer wants to tell us something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, tomorrow is the due date for Prosecution response to a motion for reconsideration that's been filed by the Prlic team. It was the motion for reconsideration was filed on the 4th of June. It's in reference to documents related to the Defence expert Milan Cvikl, and tomorrow is the due date for the Prosecution response. Now, as the Trial Chamber and the parties are aware, there have been a number of decisions filed by the Trial Chamber today in respect of release issues, and in fact on one of those the Prosecution was asked to file an urgent response today, which we've done, but all of that has sort of distracted us from some of the other filings that we've been working on, and the request is to ask for permission to file our response to this Cvikl motion on Monday of next week. I've conferred with Mr. Karnavas and there is no objection to that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes. Taking account of the fact that the Chamber gave a number of decisions and there was an urgent motion, the Chamber understands very well that you couldn't do normally your job and that we will give you until Monday for answering to the Prlic motion. You have until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understand that we have a colossal rhythm. You see the number of decisions we have to give every day, so we are close to an overdose, and the urgent motions which are received at the last minute. Right. So, Mr. Praljak, we'll continue. Unfortunately, I think we're lagging behind a bit. I was hoping to finish tomorrow, but it's clear I won't be able to finish tomorrow. It's said that you instigated, facilitated, and encouraged the obstruction of humanitarian assistance to Bosnian Muslims by not exerting your authority to effect a constant and uninterrupted flow of humanitarian assistance including to east Mostar where your lack of action resulted in substantially blocking all humanitarian aid in July and August 1993. So this is a matter we know well. We don't need to show you documents about this, on this point, and -- so this is one of the counts of the Prosecution in its pre-trial brief. What do you have to answer to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in actual fact, nothing. You've seen it all. You have the documents. You were able to see how many times I issued orders not to interfere with humanitarian aid and assistance. You saw me up on the APC when I let them go through despite the people who wanted to stop it going through for their own reasons. You have the documents, the latest statement from me, the fact that I replaced the leadership in Vakuf when I suspected that they might have stopped humanitarian assistance from going through at the point in time when the combat had stopped and about the 15th of August. This is 1993 when that convoy passed through. It never ever happened that humanitarian assistance did not get to where it was going. Sometimes in the most infinitesimal percentages some idiot would try to do that, but nobody stopped a single humanitarian convoy from getting through, and you saw my input in all that based on the documents. So I have nothing further to say. Humanitarian aid, wounded, and everything else. I've said it all. You've seen it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... also says that you participated in the seizure of movable and immovable property and transfer of its ownership to the Herceg-Bosna HVO military. So you would have participated to everything which has been mentioned in -- by the witnesses, people's whose flats were taken away from them, persons who obviously were -- saw their money and their cars and their wallets taken away, stolen from them, and this is what is meant by this text. What is -- what do you have to say about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, my -- it's difficult for me to give an answer because I just can't understand the allegations that are made. You saw how I behaved in Rama. You saw all the documents about that. So I never had anything to do with any of those allegations, and it never ever happened that I would allow something like that to be done. I wouldn't sanction it -- or, rather, I did sanction it. I fought. Well, I have nothing further to say. Let them show a single document. It's very difficult for me to talk about things like that. I didn't, I did not, and I did not once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution says that you also participated in a joint criminal enterprise in the perpetration of the crimes alleged in the indictment. You facilitated in these matters, you supported them and encouraged them by planning, approving, preparing, supporting, ordering and/or directing military operations and actions during and as part of which cultural and religious property such as mosques were destroyed and private property of Bosnian Muslims was looted, burnt, or destroyed without justification or military necessity, and failing to prevent, stop, or punish or redress such destruction and looting. Destructions, therefore, of mosques, destruction of buildings belonging to private persons, looting of the goods of Bosnian Muslims. You're alleged to have facilitated, supported, encouraged all this. And in your capacity of superior person responsible under Article 7(3), you would have done nothing to prevent or to punish the authors of this -- these destructions, or looting, or to remedy to stop that. This is reproached to you in very general terms. Therefore, General Praljak, what would you answer to this without any -- any need for us to pull out some documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- or, rather, none of this is correct or true, none of it. The mosques that are stipulated was -- is incorrect. They were already destroyed by the Serbs. We've seen that. I never issued any orders, either written or oral to that effect. They knew what my position was in the minutest detail. No action was ever launched except for military defence, and I reject and refute all these allegations that have been listed here without any proof whatsoever. It was quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, still according to the Prosecution you would have participated and supported a system of ill-treatment conceived and achieved to evict or transfer forcibly many Muslims of Bosnia and to facilitate and to support the system by deporting them out of Bosnia-Herzegovina to other countries or transferring them to parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina not claimed or not controlled by Herceg-Bosna or HVO forces, which included your proposal that Bosnian Muslims be expelled from the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna during the war between the HVO and ABiH. So this is a very long sentence, but you have understood that it is a question that has to do with the Muslims who would be deported, evicted from their homes and will have to leave their home and will find themselves in this or that area and for some of them in Croatia or other countries, third countries. There are several facets. You have already studied and spoken on this matter. What do you have to say on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reject it wholly, except that I had refugees. Well, I should have expelled them first and killed them in my weekend cottage, and dozens of -- and dozens and dozens of them passed through my flat in Zagreb, and a witness will be coming in to state his views about that while I was Chief of the Main Staff down there. Ninety-eight percent was devoted to the defence against the Muslim onslaught that began before the 24th, but I'm counting as of the 24th to the 8th, ceaselessly without interruption with the wish to route us. All my energy, 99 percent of my energy, was spent in holding the lines and preventing their onslaught. I did that, and so did all my fellow commanders. So none of what the Prosecutor alleges here is true and correct. Except for the fact that I can say that even under those conditions in West Mostar, for example, this kind of thinking and dissemination of information was that 7.000 Muslims lived there and several thousand Serbs lived there, which is -- which are figures not recorded anywhere else, although certain individuals did during the night do things that were contrary to the law. But to say that the HVO or Slobodan Praljak or anybody else did what the Prosecutor alleges, then 7.000 Muslims wouldn't have received assistance and lived in West Mostar along with several thousand Serbs. So it was our policy, including the policy of the soldiers and commanders of the HVO, was to look at the problems, and had that been our view we could have solved the problem in two days. But no, no, and I state again no, we did not do any of what is alleged there, which doesn't mean to say that individuals or groups who were out of control might have done something, but then that requires an investigation and inquiries into who the perpetrators were, whereas the merit for seeing that 7.000 Muslims did live there along with several thousand Serbs is thanks to us. And I'm proud of that, quite contrary to the allegations made here, because I contributed to the fact that those people lived there along with my commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution indicates that you were responsible for ensuring that the HVO armed forces conducted themselves in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law and that all prisoners, detainees and other persons held by the HVO armed forces, were treated in compliance with such conventions and law, and that you failed to do so, and to support this the Prosecution indicates -- that there is a document we are now going to see, P5188. This is an order which you just signed -- which you have signed as a military [indiscernible], applying an order given from -- by Mr. Boban. You had instructions from him which are to be found in several paragraphs. According to this, if I understand rightly, there's something missing in this document, some references to the respect of international conventions, applying these conventions, so what can you say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you -- well, I was in the IPD, and it was transferred to the HVO. If you gave out thousands of instructions on the subject, if you held seminars -- I wrote documents and reports on international conventions and international law. So if you did that, which is what I did, then you did your utmost to ensure that each and every soldier knows full well what he is allowed to do and what he is not allowed to do. Every soldier, every NCO, and every officer. And you can't keep repeating this then in every order. You can't refer to humanitarian law in each and every order. Everybody was well-versed with that. And then you have military orders. And in a civilian society you can't keep repeating the same thing over and over again. You can't say you're going on a trip, but you have to stick to traffic rules. You'd learn that once you learn to drive a car. You'd pass your test and then you go ahead and bear all that in mind. So that's what I did in the HVO and in the HV, and you had many documents before you to bear that out, referring to the International Red Cross and so on. So umpteen times we did everything within our power. And orally, I don't even need to tell you how many times I repeated this to everybody, that war must be conducted in a chivalrous fashion and that we must not do that. This -- there were articles in the "Hrvatski Vojnik," "Croatian Soldier," so I emphatically reject all accusations on that level. What does it say here? This is one of Mate's orders or what is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to finish with this chapter, it is also said that you participated in the commission of crimes by the forces of Herceg-Bosna and HVO against Bosnian Muslim and instigated, encouraged, facilitated, and condoned by failing to prevent and punish such crimes by -- and by commending, rewarding, promoting, or leaving in place HVO officers and soldiers who committed or played a role in such crimes. Now, in clear terms, Prosecution reproaches you for when sometimes crimes occurred, instead of punishing the perpetrators, some of them were promoted, got promotion, whether officers or soldiers, that they were rewarded. What do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can with certainty say that I never commended anyone for anything. When people did something good, I don't remember ever signing any commendation for anyone. I think it was everybody's duty to do the best they could. That's the first point. Secondly, I didn't have the right, nor did I promote any officer. Not because of what the Prosecutor is saying, but for anything else. I don't remember every -- ever signing a chit saying this promotes someone to something. I don't know how the Prosecutor can write something like that without showing documents and saying, "Here, you did this," "There you did that." Your Honours, this is quite unacceptable. It is below any acceptable limit for any trial. It's just not true. Who? Where? What? When? Except for putting my life in jeopardy to prevent some idiot doing anything. And now -- well, I point a pistol at some idiot, and once I have run the risk of having some idiot kill me, then, on the other hand, I say, "Okay. I'm going to commend you for having mistreated someone over there." I just can't follow and understand the logic of all this. There is no logic. Honourary Prosecution, there is no elementary logic here. You are behaving as if you were Gods, as if you didn't mind whether you were dealing with men, anthropoid monkeys, rats or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... individual members of the Prosecution team or the Prosecution collectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, don't look at Mr. Stringer, who to my knowledge was not one of the drafters of the indictment. He arrived later. He's just doing his job like everybody here is doing their job. So look at me. Look at me and tell me that you challenge what has been said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the -- everyone has been speaking at the same time, and the words said by Mr. Stringer are reported in a very mutilated way. I think you have the right to make your record and to say the full sentence so that it is retained in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. The objection was to the witness's addressing individual members of the Prosecution team in the way that he has. It's our position that he can certainly comment on the indictment as he's being -- as he's doing, but attacks or -- or comments on individual members of the Prosecution team are not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, to equalise, I think Mr. Praljak has also spoken too fast. So in the transcript I do not find the name of any member of the Prosecution team. So I think that we can go on then and leave that as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I am now going to examine in detail with several documents the contents of paragraph 232 of the indictment, which is important according to me, and it would be useful to have -- to know of your own point of view. Paragraph 232 of the pre-trial brief, the Prosecutor writes this: "The HV and the HVO were acting as a military organisation, a single, a unified military organisation." So we're going now to have a look at two documents. First of all P00156. This is a document we've already seen but which fits in the framework of what is said here. Now, you know this document. President Tudjman appoints Mr. Bobetko as commander of all the units of the Croatian army for the southern front, from Split to Dubrovnik, and the Croatian navy is subordinated to him. Now, on this document which we have already seen, what can you tell us? Does this fit the theory of the Prosecution according to which the HV and the HVO were a single and unified military organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see a reference here to the HVO. There's no reference for the HVO. I apologise. Mr. Stringer, I really didn't mean you personally, and please accept my apology. No. This is an order issued by Franjo Tudjman for the southern theatre of war in Croatia, from Split to Dubrovnik. And if you take into account everything that has been clearly demonstrated in this courtroom about the intents of the JNA and about what was going on, he says in very simple terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the second document which will shed light on the former. P00170. In this document, which was created on the 21st of April, 1992, while the first document was the 10th of April, that is 11 days later, Mr. Bobetko, who is the commander for the southern front, sends this document to Mr. Roso and to Mr. Miljenko Crnjac. Excuse my pronunciation. And he indicates that Major General Ante Roso is responsible for the region of Livno. Then I'm trying to understand. Livno is in Croatia or in the Republic of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honour. This order --

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How is it that General Bobetko, who is a general in the Croatian army, he has a territorial area that falls within his remit, an area which belongs to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he wants all the reports to be sent to the IZM of Grude.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what I have already said about General Bobetko. He did not have the right to sign this, not in this form. He should have assisted. However, he was not allowed to issue any orders. Nevertheless, General Bobetko simply -- for him the -- the borders did not mean much, and in that respect he wanted to be actually greater than he was, hence the misunderstandings as I explained them. He had a lot of misunderstandings with me because I didn't any recognise of such things, and he issued an order to me and asked for reports that he never received from me. This was an unlawful interference that lasted for a while until the moment General Petkovic took over command in his own way. However, it is also true that taking into account his advanced age, General Petkovic had a much harder time opposing General Bobetko than I did, because as I've already told you, people were tolerant of elderly men irrespective of the fact that they violated their rights. Franjo Tudjman appoint him very precisely to be in charge of the area between Split and Dubrovnik, and he could coordinate tasks in that area. But you know, some people want to be greater than they actually are. He was not in a position to sign this order. He did, and now what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a look at paragraph 232.15, which discusses Roso's position. P09596. You can see this document which comes from the Republic of Croatia. It concerns Mr. Roso, because on the 20th of October, 1993, it is stated that Mr. Roso's active military service comes to an end, and he is removed on the 15th of October and is relieved of his duty. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know, Your Honour. I don't know anything. I saw the documents among the documents before, I suppose. It is possible that -- look, I've already made some indications that after the Muslim offensive I would be looking as a result of some discourse that I've already spoken about that I would leave the area, and there was also a problem that I've already spoken about, and if you will allow me to share this with you. You know, in order to do certain things well, in a military generals should not be so close to so many soldiers. However, given the nature of the -- of the war and the situation at hand that was rather bad, I already came to know at least one-third of the soldiers who were deployed. And if you will allow me, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you will remember the document that I reported, the elements of the volunteers from the 5th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, to interrupt you, but since I'm also an elderly man, you may probably accept, because we spoke -- you spoke about elderly men like General Bobetko, and I'm also an elderly man, so I hope you will accept my advice that really you have to talk about the subject matter and to talk about the question which President Antonetti asked you, because really sometimes you are going beyond the -- I would say the limits of the question concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I cautioned you at the beginning of the afternoon already. Please provide brief and short answers. This is in the interest of everybody, because if in your answers there are things which are not useful, this is detrimental to everyone. My questions tend to be lengthy because I want you to understand what it is I'm getting at. Sometimes, unfortunately, I don't achieve this, which may explain why your answers are longer than what I expect. I'm trying to do my best. Another document which is a similar document. It's P06520 [as interpreted], which concerns you, as a matter of fact. This document P06521. It's the same as a 3D00280, 280. This document is a document that relieves you of your duty. It's a document we've seen already. As the document states, because of your state of health you are relieved as of the 24th of October, 1993. This document, when you compare it with the document that discusses Mr. Roso, a reasonable trier of fact could infer that the HVO officers, some of them at any rate, are officers of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is correct. Not at the same time though. Not at the same time. When I was in the Croatian army, I was in the Croatian army. When I was in the HVO, I was in the HVO. Those were two different militaries which coordinated certain things which were precisely described, and there's nothing to add to that. I repeat: The same was present in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it came to serving in the Croatian army. There was no difference there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to get back to General Roso and look at document P00195. Here we have it. The first article is what I'm interested in. I would like you to provide us with your comments. It states that: "The only legal military units in the territory of the HZ HB are the units of the HVO." This is what he says. Do you agree with him or don't you agree? Has he made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wrong. I don't agree. He should not have written that. It was beyond the -- his remit, but General Roso issued some other orders which were not within his remit. Besides, at that particular moment he was the commander of the operation zone in Livno, and he did not have any competencies that would allow him to write something like this. The Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO at the time was General Petkovic, and General Roso did not have any right whatsoever to say who was legal and who was not. First of all, he could not do it as a member of the military, because that was a civilian problem, not a military problem, but that was his problem, you know, and has nothing whatsoever to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall look at document P00197. This is a document we've seen already briefly. I'm sure you remember this document, don't you, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document earlier in this courtroom, and I know nothing about the document or the events that it describes, none whatsoever. I don't have anything to do -- I didn't have anything to do with Busovaca. I don't -- I'm not sure whether at the time I was even in command of the zone, and I don't think I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is dated the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, Your Honours, that from the 10th of April for a while I was the commander of the operative zone in Mostar. At that time I wasn't even that. So what I'm saying is that I don't have any direct or indirect connection with this document, and I can't provide any comments upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is signed by Mr. Kordic. What I'm interested in is the first article where it says that the agreement between the HVO and the so-called Busovaca TO is terminated. In paragraph 3, it states all paramilitary formations of the TO are -- must hand in their weapons. So this is why there is an ultimatum. And he adds that an arrest warrant has been issued against three people, including the famous Merdan. On the face of this document, could we say that part of the HVO or a group of individuals, I don't know, feel that -- that they are the only ones there and that the others don't count, and the Territorial Defence of Busovaca is completely sidelined? What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document speaks about that, but first it says that they were attacked. An agreement had been reached between the HVO and the TO Busovaca on everything, but then an attack ensued, and that was part of the tactic of the TO forces. There were always minor things. Somebody was brought in, somebody was being beaten up. And then the reactions on the Croatian side were sometimes inproportionate, there is no doubt about that, but there was always a kind of creeping aggression which took very small steps, and then when things accumulated the other side reacted nervously. That's correct. However, while I was there this was taken care of. Towards the end of 1992, the BiH army cooperated relatively well with the HVO except for Crljenica and so on and so forth. It depending largely from one place to another, from one person to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 232.18. The Prosecutor states that Tudjman shared the military responsibility -- I shall repeat and read it out slowly. In paragraph 232.18, it states and the Prosecutor says, and I am quoting: "Tudjman shared military responsibility in Herceg-Bosna between the generals of the HV and the HVO and even prepared plans for the HVO in the absence of any member of the HVO." To illustrate this point, we shall look at document P06831, which is a transcript from a meeting of the 23rd of November, 1993. You are no longer holding a position. We know this. Let's look at page 7 of the English version. Page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Would you happen to have the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the page number, there are a lot of figures here. 0132-3000 to 100, 3100, 0032-3126. We have the text before us now. I noted the following: Tudjman takes the floor at one point - this is in the middle of the document - and he talks about the Mostar bridge and you can see that he says that it is a fiasco, and he puts a question and says, Who ordered the destruction of the bridge and why was this done? Clearly the -- clearly President Tudjman had not ordered the destruction of the bridge. It seems that he -- it comes out of the blue for him. And he puts a question, and Susak answers, and we don't know what he answers because paper can be heard, rustling of paper. This is strange, and we don't know. Mr. Praljak, you who are very familiar with the way the political and military structures operate, when Mr. Tudjman says that he is discovering that the Mostar bridge was destroyed, is this plausible or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He learned that the bridge had been destroyed on the day. He was watching TV, of course. But he for many reasons, and I know because I've read everything, he was angry for several reasons. I can share them with you if you want me to do so. He asks here who has inflicted this terrible damage, because the whole world was aware of the fact that the HVO was the one responsible. My name already came into play, and he wanted to know who it was. Just in passing, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, sometime before 2000 I wrote to UNESCO asking them to launch an investigation about the Old Bridge. It just occurred to me subsequently that this happened. But nobody could care less about that request. So really he didn't have a clue who it was who destroyed the Old Bridge. And he's also here angry about some other things, because Bobetko had signed an order that he should not have signed as I have just explained to you a while ago. He signed an order on behalf of Franjo Tudjman and the ministry concerning Prozor. Although in the previous sentences and previous agreements Franjo Tudjman told him clearly, Yes, volunteers from the Croatian army will be rewarded if they go down there and try to put a stop on the Muslim offensive near Vakuf and break a corridor towards Central Bosnia. And believe me, one of the people who were in charge of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and the president says here one of the co-presidents asked me if we were able to defend Gornji Vakuf. One of the co-chairpersons of the conference. And this could have been Stoltenberg who asked him, Okay, if you are defeated by the Muslims what kind of a plan can we come up with if you're stuck by Vakuf and if we strike a balance then we will have a political force to ask them to do something. This is this political military game which is complicated, and all the big players in that game were outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your counsel needs to take the floor. I shall mention paragraph 132, and then by way of a transition I shall mention the transcripts in which your name is mentioned. I will then address the presidential transcripts, and I will finish off with your case which you state in your submissions which you filed in April and quote the documents that you mention. This will -- we will not finish tomorrow undoubtedly, probably on Monday. I would like to move on faster, but you answer slowly. So we're running behind time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Paragraph 232.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree. I can't be any shorter. Please don't force me to cut myself short. I'm really trying very hard to reduce my words to a minimum, but this was complicated. If a co-chairperson asked Tudjman to stop them near Vakuf, this is an important piece of information. Please don't ask me to do that. I've been here for five years. I'm defending my honour. Allow me to do so. If we have time do so, we have to make time if we don't have the time. We can stay here for two years searching for the truth for -- for the sake of God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. Praljak. I know that you are putting a great deal of effort into this, and so are we all, but the clock is ticking and we can't spend 20 years here because in 20 years I won't be here anymore. You have the floor. Let's move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
